Photograph: Johnny Greig/AlamyRenting propertyCost of renting in Britain to rise twice as fast as buying amid shortage of propertiesRents to rise by 14% until at least 2029, Hamptons predicts, as high demand for properties and low supply push up costs for tenants

Prefer the Guardian on GoogleThe cost of renting a home in Britain is expected to rise about twice as fast as that of buying one until at least 2029, according to research, with shrinking supply pushing up the prices paid by tenants.

Rents on newly agreed lets are forecast to grow by 14.2% between 2026 and 2029, compared with house price growth of 7.2%, according to forecasts from estate agent Hamptons.

It said it expected growth in rents to peak at 4.5% in 2027 across Great Britain, before growing by an estimated 3.5% in 2028 and 2.5% in 2029.

Read moreThe supply of homes available to rent is expected to remain under pressure as landlords face higher costs and tighter regulation. Rents are usually set by the balance between supply and demand, and fewer rental homes will keep upward pressure on what landlords charge.

The number of rental homes available in October was 26% lower than a decade earlier, the research found, while there had been an even sharper 39% fall in London over the same period.

At the same time, affordability pressures affecting would-be buyers has maintained demand for rental homes, with 10% more people hoping to rent a property in October compared with a year earlier.

“The central challenge facing the rental market is increasingly one of supply,” said Aneisha Beveridge, head of research at Hamptons.

She added that landlords have historically had limited opportunity to pass on higher costs to tenants: “But as costs have risen across the sector and rental supply has fallen, the bar has shifted, allowing more of those increases to feed through into higher rents.”

The number of rental homes available has been squeezed by regulatory changes under the Renters’ Rights Act, while higher tax and mortgage rates over the last decade represent about £900 a tenancy in England each year, equivalent to 18% of rental growth over that period.

Rising rents mean buying a home is cheaper than being a tenant across seven of the UK’s 12 big cities outside London, according to separate research by Lloyds bank.

Lloyds found the biggest savings were in Glasgow, Scotland, where mortgage repayments were £288 a month lower than average rents, based on data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) and the monthly cost of a 95% mortgage with an interest rate of at 5.82%, arranged over 30 years.

Estimated monthly mortgage payments were also cheaper than average rent in Newcastle, Bristol, Belfast, Nottingham and Manchester, while the analysis found there was a minimal saving to be made by buying instead of renting in Edinburgh.

However, the UK’s largest mortgage lender found monthly rent payments were cheaper than mortgage repayments in cities including Leeds, Liverpool, Birmingham and Cardiff.

Andrew Asaam, mortgages director at Lloyds, said: “For anyone weighing up whether to carry on renting or take the plunge and buy, the monthly costs really matter. Higher mortgage rates have seen the cost of borrowing increase this year, making that affordability calculation even more important.”

He added: “Even where the mortgage costs a little more, every repayment chips away at the amount owed and builds up the owner’s stake in their home. For those planning to stay put for several years, that can make a real difference over time.”
